samples.refined_query: Show the names and countries of singers who performed in concerts in 2014.
samples.sql: SELECT DISTINCT s.Name, s.Country FROM singer s JOIN singer_in_concert sic ON s.Singer_ID = sic.Singer_ID JOIN concert c ON sic.concert_ID = c.concert_ID WHERE c.Year = 2014
samples.expected_reasoning: [OK] Validation: APPROVED. All columns (Name, Country, Singer_ID, concert_ID, Year) exist in the APS schema. Both JOINs use valid ON clauses. DISTINCT is correctly applied because the bridge table singer_in_concert can produce duplicate singer rows. WHERE filters on concert.Year = 2014, which matches the user's intent. No forbidden constructs detected.

samples.refined_query: List all song names by singers above the average age.
samples.sql: SELECT Song_Name FROM singer WHERE Age > (SELECT AVG(Age) FROM singer)
samples.expected_reasoning: [OK] Validation: APPROVED. Song_Name and Age exist in the APS schema for singer. The correlated subquery computes AVG(Age) over the same table, which directly matches the user's intent of 'above the average age'. No SELECT *, no DML, no forbidden constructs. The subquery is a scalar aggregate — not a performance risk for small tables.

samples.refined_query: Show the names of singers who have not performed in any concert.
samples.sql: SELECT Name FROM singer WHERE Singer_ID NOT IN (SELECT Singer_ID FROM singer_in_concert)
samples.expected_reasoning: [OK] Validation: APPROVED. Name and Singer_ID exist in singer; Singer_ID exists in singer_in_concert. NOT IN with a scalar subquery correctly implements exclusion semantics — singers absent from singer_in_concert have not performed. This directly answers 'who have not performed in any concert'. No forbidden constructs detected.

samples.refined_query: Show stadium names and the highest year of concerts held in each stadium.
samples.sql: SELECT T2.name, MAX(T1.year) FROM concert AS T1 JOIN stadium AS T2 ON T1.stadium_id = T2.stadium_id GROUP BY T1.stadium_id, T2.name
samples.expected_reasoning: [OK] Validation: APPROVED. year and stadium_id exist in concert; name and stadium_id exist in stadium. JOIN ON stadium_id is valid. MAX(year) correctly answers 'highest year'. GROUP BY includes both T1.stadium_id and T2.name — all non-aggregated SELECT columns are in GROUP BY, satisfying MySQL 8.0 ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY mode. No forbidden constructs.

samples.refined_query: What percentage of singers are male?
samples.sql: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN is_male = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS DOUBLE) * 100 / COUNT(singer_id) FROM singer
samples.expected_reasoning: [OK] Validation: APPROVED. is_male and singer_id exist in the APS schema. CAST AS DOUBLE is valid MySQL syntax for floating-point division. CASE WHEN correctly counts male singers (is_male=1) and divides by total COUNT(singer_id) — this produces the percentage the user asked for. No SELECT *, no DML, no forbidden constructs.
